messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun Mehta was a 41-year-old South Asian park ranger who had been in a steady relationship for several years and, until recently, had prided himself on being calm, practical, and hard to rattle. That changed after a period of captivity overseas, an experience he still described only in fragments because the full account felt too shameful and too close. What stayed with him were not stories in sequence but a set of snapshots: a metal door half open, the glare of a fluorescent light, a boot stepping into view, the hard grip on his arm, and the taste of fear in his mouth. Whenever those details were sparked by a military comment on television or the sight of uniforms at the trailhead, Arjun found himself immediately thinking that the world was not safe and that he had been foolish, weak, and uniquely unfortunate. Those conclusions made the memory more vivid and easier to find, as if the snapshots waited just beneath the surface whenever he judged himself that way. When those images came back, they did so as if they were happening in the room with him; at times he could feel the old ache and pressure in the same parts of his body, and at other times he could describe the scene with a flat, numbed distance, as though it had happened to someone else. Even in the early weeks after he returned home, unexpected movement nearby made him flinch as though he were back in danger, and he could not trust reassurance. Because he had come to believe the world was unsafe and that he could not trust his own judgment, almost anything could serve as a trigger: a boot on a trail, a uniform at work, a voice raised on the television, or someone moving too quickly in his peripheral vision. Each of those moments seemed to confirm the same bleak conclusion, and the more certain he became of that conclusion, the more sensitive he was to the next cue. Friends told him he was safe; his partner said the doors were locked; Arjun still scanned the room, convinced that safety could be taken away without warning. He also began to feel permanently humiliated by what had happened, certain that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, and the humiliation deepened his sense that he was set apart from everyone around him. That humiliation made him more alert to possible signs that it could happen again; once he had decided he could not trust his own judgment, a raised voice, a stranger turning too quickly, or a uniform in the wrong place could all snag his attention and feel like proof that danger was nearby.

Those appraisals quickly shaped how he moved through the world. Arjun came to believe that being seen carried risk, so he made himself smaller in public, avoided eye contact, and went along with whatever others wanted because agreeing felt safer than being noticed. He also imposed strict control over what he ate, cutting portions and skipping meals because regulating food gave him one area where he could feel disciplined and not at the mercy of anyone else. The memory would come back when he was trying to keep himself controlled, and after it surfaced he would tighten those routines further, telling himself that if he could just stay disciplined enough he might keep the images at bay. But the more he skipped meals and deferred to others, the more he felt that he needed those habits, and the more his life seemed to map itself around the captivity he was trying not to think about. At the same time, he found himself replaying scenes of revenge against the people responsible, imagining power reversed and himself no longer trapped. Those scenes were not just fantasies for him; they were what he turned to when the memory broke through, a way of keeping the event in view without feeling helpless inside it. Even so, each time he returned to them, the captivity felt nearer and more dangerous, and he came away thinking that he must still be deeply changed by it. Yet these efforts never settled him for long. The more he tried to control his eating, please others, or mentally punish his captors, the more the images returned in sharper pieces, each flash of the event seeming to confirm how isolated and humiliated he had become. That constant sense of danger was itself part of the problem: when he felt most on edge, the snapshots came back with extra force, as if his body’s alarm were pulling him closer to the moment rather than away from it. Feeling that threatened also made him more certain that the event had permanently altered him and that safety was something other people got, not him. The memory was especially liable to be pulled loose by military topics; if someone at home mentioned the army, or if a news report showed uniforms, his mind jumped straight back to those few terrible moments. Uniforms also set off the same reaction at work, where, as a park ranger, he sometimes encountered law enforcement or search-and-rescue personnel in similar clothing. Being seen in those moments felt exposing, and once he was self-conscious under someone’s gaze, he would think again that he had been foolish, weak, and uniquely unfortunate, which only made the old images more vivid and shameful.

As the months passed, the memory itself started to drive the rest of the cycle. A sudden return of the snapshot images could bring a wave of bodily pain and make him feel as if the captivity were happening again, and once that threat feeling rose he became even more certain that he could not trust safety. When he was jolted by a sound or an abrupt movement on a trail, the room or forest seemed to tilt toward the past, and that sense of danger made the fragments of memory sharper still. The memories, in turn, fed back into his negative beliefs: each return seemed to prove that he remained isolated, permanently humiliated, and somehow at fault. Because he felt that way, he redoubled his efforts to keep control, eating even more strictly, deferring to others, and fantasizing about revenge in private. But these strategies brought their own costs. Skipping meals left him shaky and more reactive to sudden movement, which made the world feel even less safe. Going along with everyone else left him resentful and more aware of being unseen. Revenge fantasies kept his mind circling the captivity long after work, making the images easier to summon and the humiliation harder to shake. And once he was already keyed up, even a uniform at the trailhead, a military comment on television, or a stranger turning too quickly on the path could trigger the same surge of dread and pull him back into the snapshots again.

By the time he sought help, Arjun was still functioning at work but only by keeping himself tightly managed and on edge. His partner had noticed that he was distant at home, jumpy when someone moved unexpectedly, and increasingly unwilling to go out unless he could control the setting. What finally brought him in was the fear that he was becoming trapped in the same private loop every day: the images, the humiliation, the rigid control, the constant scanning. He said he was most afraid that the captivity had permanently changed him, but he was also hoping that therapy might help him feel safe enough to stop living as if danger were always one step away.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows triggers bringing back the memory, but does not clearly state that triggers directly drive negative appraisals in the same causal sequence.
It describes negative beliefs making him more alert to cues, but does not clearly show negative appraisals causing triggers to appear or become active.
It shows appraisals shaping his behavior, but not that the appraisals directly lead to the maladaptive strategies in a clearly stated causal way within a single paragraph for this edge.
The memory is described as worsening his beliefs, but the specific causal link from memory to negative appraisals is not explicitly conveyed in the same paragraph.
The memory is said to be triggered by cues, but there is no clear statement that the memory itself causes new triggers to arise.
Although threat feelings are linked to the memory, the vignette does not clearly state that threat directly brings back the memory in a causal chain.
The strategies are described as responses to the memory or beliefs, but the vignette does not clearly state that the maladaptive strategies directly cause the memory to recur.
The strategies are said to have costs, but the vignette does not clearly state that they directly generate or intensify the negative appraisals in a causal sequence.
The vignette does not explicitly show the maladaptive strategies producing new triggers or increasing cue sensitivity in a direct causal relationship.
While he becomes more reactive and the world feels less safe, the vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies directly increase threat in a causal chain.
